title: Cold Mecha
mood: A mended servo, a stall at the city’s edge, and a small director who wants to watch Selena work.

hero.alt: Design sheet of one of the Academy's AI droids: a slim white machine with a single orange eye and long jointed arms, a spare arm and close views of its head drawn beside it.

segs.t: The droid sat slumped on the bench beside Selena, its right arm dead from the shoulder down.
It was one of the Academy’s helpers, slim and white, with one orange eye.
Selena laid the arm across her knees, put two fingers on the casing and shut her eyes.
Current ran under her fingertips toward the wrist. Halfway there it stopped, and that place felt cold and still.
The pull toward the bay was stronger than it had been in the workshop. She kept her fingers on the casing.
She opened the casing over the cold place. Inside a sleeve, a wire had cracked, finer than a hair. She bridged it.
The arm jerked and flexed its fingers. The droid’s orange eye blinked on.
Mr. Bunny’s black screen showed two round eyes.
“Three of us spent two days on that arm,” said Chang’e from her stool. She held up two jelly candies, then closed her fist on them. “You still haven’t told me where you learned that trick.”
“Here and there.”
On the shelf above the bench stood an old servo in a little wire stand. Its arm turned slowly back and forth. One corner of the casing was still black.
Selena knew that soot. She had pulled the servo out of the ash herself.
Terrinia. The year the base fell.
The sirens went. Karina already had her boots on.
“Door locked,” she said, and was gone down the stair.
Selena locked the door behind her and climbed to the roof.
Half the city was burning: the far half, where the research base stood. Smoke rolled up red into the dark.
Something walked through the middle of the fire. It was black and gold, and taller than the towers around it.
Its hum reached her across the whole city. It rang in her bones the way a bell rings after the blow.
It feels like the first night.
Her hands closed on the rail of the water tank.
Once, a white light opened in its chest. Far off, a street went white. Then it went dark.
Karina went that way.
She watched until the giant turned back into the smoke and the ringing went out of her bones. Then she went down and sat at the table, where Karina had left her.
Karina came back the next afternoon and fell asleep at the table with her helmet on. Selena lifted it off her and set it by the door.
Days later the scavengers came to the base’s ruins, and she came with them.
They picked through the burned buildings at its edge with sacks and hooks. Half of them were children.
A boy with a hook looked her over. “You’re new. Hooks are extra.”
She used her hands.
In a storehouse with no roof, under a fallen rack, she found a servo, black at one corner. Across its base ran a strip of label tape, written on in a small quick hand.
At the flat she wired it to an old radio battery and held it in both hands.
Somewhere inside, the current stopped short. She could feel where, the way she felt an Ender’s hum. No book had taught her that.
She opened it at the dead place and found the crack. By morning its arm turned back and forth on the table.
A week later the Shield put guards on the ruins. The scavengers moved on, and Selena with them. She sold what she mended to the workshops on the outskirts.
The servo she kept.
On storm nights now she went further than the roof.

She slipped into the shady streets of the outskirts. On a stranger’s roof she folded the coat Karina made her wear and tucked it under a water tank. She let the purple spread over her arms and legs. Then she raced through the city like a shadow, free to go wherever she pleased.
One night, after a raid, the Enders were gone and smoke lay low on the wet streets.
Under the rain, somebody was crying.
A shop front had come down. A small boy lay in the street with its iron shutter across his leg. Two streets off, rescue lamps were moving away.
Selena called the purple back under her skin and climbed down.
The boy had his face pressed into his arm against the rain.
She slid one hand under the shutter. It felt light. Light enough to press down instead.
She lifted. It came up off his leg. Two grown men could not have shifted it.
She bent to his ear. “Shh. It won’t hurt anymore.”
He dragged his leg free. She stood him up and turned him by the shoulders toward the lamps.
“That way. Shout.”
He limped off, shouting. The lamps turned toward him.
Before their light reached the corner, she was back on the roofs.
Three roofs later she was still asking herself why.
Nothing,
she decided.
It was nothing.
She ran on.
The years went by in plates and parts.

Her crate at the city’s edge, where the salvage crews dragged in what they found, became a trestle table under a tarp. The mended servo sat on its corner and turned its arm back and forth all day. It was her sign, priced so high that nobody ever bought it.
A workshop man once paid her for four plates and walked off with five.
The next week he wanted four more. She counted them out and held out her hand for the price of five.
“Miscounted,” she said.
He paid. By then every workshop on his street had heard about the fifth plate.
She outgrew three more pairs of boots. No buyer ever asked where a girl learned to price Ender plating.
Years after the fall, scaffolds went up on the base’s ruins. A new hall rose out of the ash, and a name went up over its gate: Selrick Academy.
On the bright morning it opened that gate, she was at the fence.
Figures in suits stood in the yard. They rose one after another on wings of light. In a line they flew over her head, out over the city, and turned toward the water.
No suit had flown over the city before that day.
“The instructors,” said a man at the fence. “Shield soldiers, in the new suits.”
People cheered. People had praised her talent all her life. Their praise never truly meant anything to her.
What fascinated her instead were the cold mecha constructs at Selrick Academy. The circuits and energy coursing through them felt far more like what flowed through her own veins.
Her fingers curled through the fence wire.
One morning a small girl stopped at Selena’s table.
She wore a white lab coat cut to child size. A white robot rabbit hung at her shoulder. She picked up the servo and watched its arm turn.
“Who mended this?”
“I did.”
“With what?”
“Hands.”
The girl turned it over. She rubbed the soot off the label tape with one finger and read the small quick writing.
“This came from my parents’ lab,” she said.
Her finger stayed on the tape after the soot was gone.
The far half,
Selena thought.
The street that went white.
The girl did not ask where she had found it.
Then she lifted her chin. “I’m Chang’e. I direct the Science Division at Selrick.”
Selena looked at the coat. “You do?”
“Since its first day.” The rabbit’s screen frowned at Selena.
Chang’e held up the servo. “How much?”
Selena tapped the tag. Chang’e counted coins onto the tarp, came up short, and laid two jelly candies beside them.
“Those aren’t money.”
“They’re better.”
Selena picked up the candies.
Chang’e tucked the servo under her arm. “The Science Division takes its entry next week. Come.”
“Why?”
“Nobody in my lab can do what you did to this. I want to watch you do it.”
Then she was gone, the rabbit bobbing after her.
Selena sat on her crate with the candies in her fist. Nobody had sent her. In those days nothing pulled at her cells at all.
I want my hands inside one of those suits.
Best tools in the city. The biggest pile of Ender wreck in it.
And nobody hunts for an Ender inside the place built to fight them.
Karina would be proud.
That last one she did not look at too closely.
Getting into the Science Division was like a children’s game to Selena. She finished the paper early and drew on its back: a small machine with four legs and a long tail.
Then came the form on the screen. Name: Selena. The family-name box she left empty.
Selena. That’s the whole name.
It glowed red.
Here it comes,
she thought. Questions, or a shut door.
Nobody said anything. The examiner took her paper and called the next name.
The results came one evening. Selena was at the table when Karina came in from her shift.
“Science Division,” said Selena.
Karina set her helmet down. She nodded twice. “I want to see you graduate.”
“That’s years.”
“I’ve got years.”
Selena went through every smile she had ever kept. None of them fit.
On her way to the sink, Karina put a fruit drop on the table by Selena’s hand.
On her first day, Selena checked her file at the Science Division door.
The family-name box was green.
She did not know who had cleared it, and she did not ask.
So it gives in,
she thought, and went inside.
The professors marveled at her instinctive understanding of the Aspirant mechas, never realizing that she herself was a living source of the technology they studied.
One of them set a dead pump on her bench and stood back to watch.
In the lab, Chang’e was still holding out her closed fist.
“Well?”
“Here and there,” said Selena again. She laid a lollipop on the bench.
Chang’e huffed and tipped the candies into Selena’s palm. She had the lollipop unwrapped before she turned back to her screen.
Selena closed her hand on them. On the shelf, the old servo turned its arm back and forth in its stand.
